prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 columns toward higher x, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting network scores 0. It learned to press DONE before placing anything, because random placements earn negative reward on average. The likely cause is the hidden rule: target, missing, extra and target-height channels are shifted 4 columns, wrapping around. The starting network only sees 2 columns either side (a 1x1 stem plus two 3x3 convs), so it cannot match the build at column x with the target shown at x+4 (or x−4 after wrap-around). With nothing it can learn, quitting is the best policy. The main fix is to give the network a circular, whole-row view along x, so it can learn the offset from data instead of having it hard-coded. A convolution with kernel (1, X) on circularly padded input can represent any wrap-around column shift and works the same at every position. Secondary risks are the early collapse to DONE and the small budget (about 32 default updates), so recipe changes are tested next to the architecture fix.

### Round 2
The 4-column wrapped shift is the main obstacle. A circular (1, X) row-conv stem fixed it: the agent went from 0 to 0.40 with the default recipe. With a smaller batch (n_envs 128) and ent_coef 0.02 it reached 0.75, and both seeds agreed (0.744 and 0.754). The best run's training curve was still rising at the end (0.53 at 75%, 0.67 at 100%) and dev IoU was 0.96, so the agent is limited by the number of updates and samples, not by perception. More frequent updates helped by about 35 points, well above the 2-seed noise. The deeper trunk with ppo_epochs 2 did badly (0.13), but it changed depth and epochs together, so ppo_epochs 2 on its own has not been tested. This round tests three ways to get more learning from the same compute: even smaller batches, fewer epochs, and a cheaper stem that only row-mixes the shifted channels.

### Round 3
The circular (1, X) row-conv stem fixes the shifted target: every circular-stem trial learned something, while the starting network scored 0. After that, the recipe gave the largest gains. Going from 256 to 128 envs raised dev success from 0.40 to 0.75. Cutting ppo_epochs from 4 to 2 raised it from 0.75 to 0.88, which is well beyond seed noise because both seeds moved. Going from 128 to 64 envs added about 4 points, within noise but in the same direction. The deeper trunk (r1c3) did worse because it was confounded with 256 envs. Sending only the shifted channels through the row conv (r2c3) was neutral. r2c2's training success was still rising at the end (0.84 to 0.89), so more samples and updates are still the main lever. The remaining mistakes are about build order, such as placing an overhang before the cells under it. A longer reward horizon may help with those.

### Round 4
The circular (1, X) row-conv stem is the key perceptual fix: it let the network undo the wrapped 4-column target shift and moved dev success from 0 to 0.40. The recipe gave the rest. n_envs 128 with ent_coef 0.02 reached 0.75, and ppo_epochs 2 on top reached 0.877 (r2c2, seeds 0.90 and 0.85). So this setup is limited by data and by the number of updates. Pushing further, with ppo_epochs 1 or n_envs 64 at epochs 2, gave a bimodal result: one seed near 0.88 and one at 0.0, which looks like early collapse. gamma 0.99 gave 0.816, which may be noise but is not better. The deeper trunk and the split stem did not help. In this last round, the 4-seed retrain rewards robustness as well as peak score. I test three single changes to r2c2: zero-initialised output layers, against collapse; a higher learning rate, for faster learning; and a slimmer row stem that brings compute to about 1x, which buys about 20% more samples.

## Trial it ended with
name: best + ppo_epochs 2
hypothesis: Same network and recipe as r1c2, but ppo_epochs is 2. That gives about 1.86 times as many environment steps (about 200k) and twice as many updates. This separates the effect of the epoch count from the deeper trunk in r1c3, which changed both. Refuted if dev success falls below about 0.70, which would mean the extra data does not make up for the weaker optimisation of each batch.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 1 gives the rule in full: "target, missing, extra and target-height channels are shifted 4 columns, wrapping around," and adds that the network "cannot match the build at column x with the target shown at x+4." This names the affected channels, the size of the shift (4), the axis and direction (toward higher x) and the wrap-around. Round 4 restates it: "undo the wrapped 4-column target shift."
